title: Bystander CPR Type and Outcomes After Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
summary: In Japan’s national registry cohort of 26,785 children with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, favorable 30-day neurological survival occurred in 16.0% with rescue-breathing CPR, 9.5% with compression-only CPR, and 3.6% without bystander CPR. Rescue-breathing CPR was associated with better neurological survival than compression-only CPR after adjustment (risk ratio 1.71, 95% CI 1.57–1.86). These associations do not establish causation.
findings: Rescue-breathing versus compression-only CPR: adjusted 30-day survival risk ratio 1.51 (95% CI 1.42–1.61).
population: Children aged 17 years or younger with known bystander-CPR status in the All-Japan Utstein Registry, 2005–2023.
shortTitle: Rescue breaths and pediatric OHCA outcomes
limitations: Nonrandomized Japanese data spanning 2005–2023 are vulnerable to confounding and changes in care. Only the primary abstract was reviewed; detailed adjustment, subgroup results, and adverse events remain unappraised.
intervention: Bystander CPR including rescue breathing (observed exposure).
whyItMatters: Supports retaining rescue breaths in pediatric CPR training; both CPR approaches were associated with better outcomes than no CPR.
evidenceNotes: Abstract reviewed through indexed primary PubMed. DOI and direct PubMed retrieval failed (Internal Error / inaccessible or Cache miss). JAMA’s official author policy confirms research is open access, but full text was not retrieved. Exact-title/DOI correction, retraction and related-evidence searches did not retrieve a target correction or later contradictory trial; this is a limited search, not proof of absence. Full-text methods and safety appraisal remain queued.
